summary: Albert Graeter (1835-1909) worked in Indology and linguistics. He served as a missionary with the Basel Mission from around 1857 to 1876 and was a teacher of English at the University of Basel from 1870 to 1908.

Albert Grünwedel (1856-1935) was a scholar of Indology, Tibetology, and archaeology. He earned his Dr. phil. at the University of Munich (1876-1883) and later served at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, including as director of the Indische Abteilung (1904-1921).
Albert Henry Allen worked in the field of Indology. He studied at the University of California, Los Angeles, earning an A.B. by 1898, and completed an M.A. at Harvard University by 1900.

Albert Henry Arden (1841-1897) worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned his B.A. from Christ's College, Cambridge, and served as University Lecturer in Telugu and Tamil at the University of Cambridge from 1882 to 1890.

Albert Henry Longhurst (1876-1955) worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied under John Marshall and served as Superintendent of the Southern Circle for the Archaeological Survey of India from 1910 to 1911.

Albert Hoefer (1812-1883) was an Indology and linguistics scholar. He studied at Greifswald, Göttingen, Berlin, and Königsberg under teachers including Bopp and Grimm. He held lecturing and professorial posts at Berlin and the University of Greifswald (~1840-1883).
Albert Hofmann (1906-2008) studied at the University of Zurich from around 1925 to 1929. He held a post at Novartis from around 1929 to 1971.

Albert Ippel (1885-1960) worked in archaeology and Indology, earning a Ph.D. at Bonn after studies at Freiburg and Berlin. He held posts at the University of Breslau, Humboldt University of Berlin, and the University of Hamburg (1947-1954).
Albert Johannes de Jong (1880-1961) was an Indologist. He studied at Utrecht University from around 1913 to 1917, completing a PhD under the supervision of Willem Caland by 1929.

Albert Joris van Windekens (1915-1989) worked in linguistics, Central Asian, and Indological studies. He studied at KU Leuven under Albert Joseph Carnoy and Jean Filliozat, later serving at KU Leuven and as director of the Centre international de dialectologie générale.

Albert Joseph Carnoy (1878-1961) was a scholar of linguistics and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied at KU Leuven (~1897-1902) and held professorships there (1904-1955), as well as posts at Columbia University and UC Berkeley.

Albert Lutz (born 1954) is a scholar in archaeology and Sinology. He studied at the University of Zurich under Eberhard Fischer and spent his career at Museum Rietberg as curator for Chinese art (1982) and director (1998-2019).

Albert Schweitzer (1875-1965) worked in philosophy and religious studies. He studied at Strasbourg, Tübingen, and the German University of Prague, studying under Wilhelm Deecke, and held an academic post at the University of Strasbourg from around 1902 to 1913.

Albert Sechehaye (1870-1946) was a linguist. He studied at the University of Geneva (~1889-1895) under Ferdinand de Saussure and later held a post at the University of Geneva from around 1903 to 1945.

Albert Socin (1844-1899) was a scholar in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the University of Basel (~1862-1866) and held posts at the Universities of Basel, Tübingen, and Leipzig.

Albert Ten Eyck Olmstead (1880-1945) worked in archaeology and Central Asian studies. After completing his Ph.D. at Cornell, he held academic posts at the University of Missouri, University of Chicago, and the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures.

Albert Thumb (1865-1915) worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied under Karl Brugmann, Hermann Osthoff, and Rudolf Thurneysen, completing his PhD at Freiburg. He held professorships at Freiburg, Marburg (1901), and Strasbourg (1909).

Albert Welter (born 1952) specializes in Buddhist studies and Sinology. He earned his PhD at McMaster University under Koichi Shinohara and held posts at the University of Winnipeg (~1995-2014) and the University of Arizona (from 2013).

Albert von Le Coq (1860-1930) worked in archaeology and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied at the Seminar for Oriental Languages (~1899-1902) and served at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin from around 1902 to 1925, becoming director in 1914.
Alberto Todeschini is a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He has held a guest post at Kyoto University and an affiliation with the Italian School of East Asian Studies attested in 2010.
